title: Meet Your Twin
subtitle: You already know how intelligence works — you live inside one.

analogy.title: AI Is Literally Your Twin
analogy.text: Every single AI buzzword you're about to hear — LLM, RAG, agents, MCP, hallucinations — literally has a human version. Not a coincidence. We built AI by copying ourselves. So before you stress about the jargon, peep how familiar it already is.

table.old: Long-term memory — recalling facts on demand
Nervous system — signals between body parts
Hands and feet — taking action in the world
Learning from mistakes — trial and error

memory_hook: AI = you, but running on silicon instead of cells. Same anatomy, different hardware.
narration: Ok look at this table for a sec. Left side: stuff about your own brain you've literally always known. Right side: the AI words that sounded like alphabet soup five minutes ago. MCP = nervous system, AI parts talking to each other. Agents = hands and feet, AI that actually DOES stuff instead of just talking. And hallucinations? That's AI dreaming — super confident, sometimes straight up making things up. Remember that last one. It's basically the whole reason the rest of this module exists.

title: The Intelligence Core
subtitle: Four pieces of machinery doing the thinking

analogy.title: What's Actually Inside the Brain
analogy.text: If the LLM is the brain, these four things are basically its different lobes, each doing its own job. None of it is magic btw — it's just pattern recognition turned up to eleven.

list.name: LLM — Large Language Model
list.desc: The brain. Predicts the next word kinda like finishing your friend's sentence — except it's read basically the whole internet to learn how.

list.name: Deep Learning
list.desc: Layered pattern recognition. Same way your brain spots a face by going edges → shapes → features, the machine does it with layers of math filters.

list.name: Transformers
list.desc: The architecture that gave AI 'attention' — like it can actually focus on what matters in a sentence instead of just reading word by word with no context.

list.name: Reinforcement Learning
list.desc: Trial and error with rewards, like how a kid learns not to touch a hot stove — except AI does millions of attempts per second.

memory_hook: LLM = brain. Deep Learning = pattern radar. Transformers = focus mode. RL = learning from L's.
narration: Let's pop the hood real quick. LLM is the main character — the brain handling language and reasoning. Deep Learning is the pattern-recognition engine, going edges → shapes → faces, exactly like your own vision works. Transformers are the 2017 glow-up that gave AI 'attention' — so it actually knows that in 'the trophy didn't fit in the suitcase because it was too big,' the 'it' means the trophy, not the suitcase. And Reinforcement Learning is just AI getting better through trial and error — like learning not to touch a hot stove, except it's running a million attempts a minute.

title: Extended Capabilities
subtitle: What lets AI act, remember, and sometimes lie

analogy.title: The Rest of the Body (and the One Thing to Watch)
analogy.text: If last slide was the brain, this slide is everything plugged into it — memory, limbs, imagination, and yeah, the dreams too. Last item on the list is the most important one. Don't skip it.

list.name: RAG — Retrieval-Augmented Generation
list.desc: Memory on demand. AI actually looks up your company's docs before answering instead of just guessing from training data.

list.name: Generative AI
list.desc: Creativity. Writing, art, code, design — actually making new stuff instead of just sorting or predicting things.

list.name: AI Agents
list.desc: Hands and feet. AI that doesn't just chat — it does stuff. Sends emails, hits databases, ships code, opens tickets.

list.name: MCP — Model Context Protocol
list.desc: The nervous system. Lets different AI parts and your existing tools all talk to each other without custom plumbing every time.

list.name: Hallucination
list.desc: AI's dream state. Confidently wrong when it doesn't actually know. The #1 risk in enterprise AI — literally why the rest of this module exists.

title: The Old World, in Three Numbers
subtitle: Why traditional software delivery is breaking

hero_stat.label: average time from kickoff to first working baseline

analogy.title: The Bus Factor (Yes, That's a Real Term)
analogy.text: Ask any PM their 'bus factor' — basically how many people getting hit by a bus would kill the project. If the answer's 1, that's not a delivery model, that's a hostage situation.

bullets: 120 days — average time just to get a baseline working. That's wild.
30–40% of effort — straight up wasted on rework and requirement chaos
1 person — the one key teammate whose vacation can stall everything

narration: Before we hype up the new way, let's be real about the old way. Three numbers tell the whole story. First: 120 days. That's the AVERAGE time just to get a working baseline on enterprise software. Four months before anyone clicks a single button. Second: 30 to 40 percent of effort straight up wasted on rework — requirements changing mid-build, surprise integration issues, docs nobody wrote. Third, and this one's scary: bus factor of one. Every big project has THAT one person whose vacation could stall everything for a week. None of this is an engineering skill issue. You can't fix it with more devs, more sprints, more frameworks. It's an orchestration problem. Needs an orchestration fix.

title: The OrchestrAI Iceberg
subtitle: What you see is days. What's underneath is years.

analogy.title: The Iceberg Effect
analogy.text: What the client actually sees is one thing — a QA-ready app in days, not months. What's hiding underneath is six layers of orchestration, built up over years. The visible part looks small because of everything happening underneath.

list.name: Layer 1 — Intent Capture
list.desc: Structured sessions that turn vague business goals into briefs AI can actually use. Runs on P.R.O.M.P.T.

list.name: Layer 2 — Pattern Library
list.desc: Pre-built, pre-tested patterns for auth, payments, reporting, workflows. AI's not reinventing the wheel — it's just assembling.

list.name: Layer 3 — AI Engine
list.desc: The generation engine. Multiple AI models working together to spit out code, schemas, UI, and tests all at once.

list.name: Layer 4 — Validation Loop
list.desc: Auto-generated tests, compliance checks, and real humans checking key spots. Quality is baked in early, not patched later.

list.name: Layer 5 — Compliance Guards
list.desc: Industry-specific rules — banking, payments, finance — checked before anything ships.

list.name: Layer 6 — Co-Working Bridge
list.desc: Daily hands-on testing with the client until they're 100% confident — then, and only then, it goes live.

memory_hook: Days of delivery you see = years of orchestration you don't.
narration: Look at an iceberg from a boat, you see a little floating chunk. Look underwater, there's like eight times more mass holding it up. Same thing with OrchestrAI. The client sees one thing — a working app in their QA space, ready in days. What's actually making that happen is six layers underneath. Intent Capture turns vague goals into precise briefs. Pattern Library means auth and payments aren't built from scratch — they're assembled from stuff that's already proven to work. AI Engine runs multiple models at once. Validation Loop bakes in quality instead of catching problems later. Compliance Guards check industry rules — huge deal in banking and payments — before anything ships. And the Co-Working Bridge is us sitting with the client every single day during UAT until they're 100% confident. The visible part's small on purpose. The hidden part is why it can be that small.

table.old: Documentation: written last, if at all

memory_hook: Same skill. Different machine. 17x faster, no cap.

title: Your New Job Description
subtitle: Three roles in one Lead

analogy.title: Triple Threat
analogy.text: You don't lose the technical skills — you just add two more on top. Strategic Advisor, Quality Guardian, Intent Translator. Most days you're wearing all three before lunch even happens.

list.name: Strategic Advisor
list.desc: You take business goals and turn them into orchestration intent. You decide what's getting built and why. CXO sees this version of you.

list.name: Intent Translator
list.desc: You turn vague requirements into precise briefs AI can actually use. P.R.O.M.P.T.'s your whole toolkit here. This is the version AI sees.

list.name: Quality Guardian
list.desc: You're not writing the code, but you own how good it is. You validate, escalate, and refuse to ship anything sloppy. Client sees this version.

title: How to Talk to AI: The P.R.O.M.P.T. Formula
subtitle: Six letters that turn AI into a senior team member

analogy.title: Architect's Brief, Not a Genie Wish
analogy.text: Hire a top architect, tell them 'make it nice' — you'll get a building, just not the one you wanted. Give them a real brief instead — purpose, role, output format, constraints, layout, tone — and you get exactly the house you pictured. P.R.O.M.P.T. is that brief, every single time.

list.name: P — Purpose
list.desc: What's the actual goal? One sentence, no fluff. ('Plan a 5-day family vacation to Bali.')

list.name: R — Role
list.desc: Who's AI pretending to be? ('Senior payments architect with 10 years at FIS.' 'Expert tour planner who knows Asia.')

list.name: O — Output
list.desc: What format do you actually need back? ('Markdown table.' 'JSON.' 'A React component.')

list.name: M — Marker
list.desc: Hard rules, non-negotiable. ('Budget ₹80k.' 'Has to follow regulation X.' 'No exceptions.')

list.name: P — Pattern
list.desc: How should it be organized? ('Day-by-day, with morning/afternoon/evening sections.')

list.name: T — Tone
list.desc: What's the vibe supposed to be? ('Friendly and casual.' 'Formal and professional.')

memory_hook: Purpose = why. Role = who. Output = shape. Marker = the rules. Pattern = the layout. Tone = the vibe.
narration: Meet your main tool. P.R.O.M.P.T. is six letters, six guardrails, and honestly the single most important skill from this whole program. Think of it like an architect's brief. title: Module 1 Knowledge Check
subtitle: 10 questions. 80% to pass. Unlimited retakes.

questions.question: Which AI thing is basically your long-term memory's twin?
questions.explanation: RAG is basically AI's long-term memory — it actually looks stuff up (like your company docs) instead of just relying on training data. From the anatomy slide: brain = LLM, long-term memory = RAG.

questions.question: AI hallucinations are basically the human version of what?
choices: Confident false memories or vivid dreams
questions.correct_answer: Confident false memories or vivid dreams
questions.explanation: Hallucinations are basically AI's dream state — vivid, confident, sometimes 100% made up. It's not lying on purpose, it just doesn't know what it doesn't know. That's exactly why P.R.O.M.P.T. exists — guardrails around what AI can and can't invent.

questions.question: How long does it usually take to get a baseline working, the old-school way?
questions.explanation: Old-school enterprise software takes 90-120 days just to get a baseline working. OrchestrAI compresses that to 7 days. That's a 17x speedup — not from working harder, just cutting work that never needed to exist.

questions.question: OrchestrAI ships to the client's ___ environment in 7 days — not straight to production.
questions.explanation: OrchestrAI delivers an 80% baseline to the client's QA in 7 days. Last 20% gets built together during UAT. Go-live only happens once the client's actually confident — not a second before. Fast, but never reckless.

questions.question: Which analogy best describes what an OrchestrAI Lead actually does?
choices: Solo violinist — total control of one instrument
Orchestra conductor — commands eighty musicians without touching one
Music critic — judges performance from the audience
Studio engineer — mixes after the recording is done
questions.correct_answer: Orchestra conductor — commands eighty musicians without touching one
questions.explanation: The conductor analogy is the main idea of this whole program. A soloist's hands are literally on the instrument. A conductor's hands touch nothing — but commands way more, through a score written with total precision beforehand. That's the shift: stop playing the instrument, start writing the score.

questions.question: Where does quality actually get built in, in the OrchestrAI model?
choices: In the QA cycle, by dedicated testers
Upstream, in the prompt and brief
questions.correct_answer: Upstream, in the prompt and brief
questions.explanation: Don't filter the river, clean the source. Old-world QA catches defects after they've already flowed through everything. OrchestrAI builds quality in upstream, in the brief itself. Every bug caught in QA traces back to a vague brief. Every compliance miss in UAT traces back to a missing Marker.

questions.question: What's the 'M' in P.R.O.M.P.T. actually stand for?
choices: Model — which AI model to use
questions.explanation: Marker = the guardrails. Hard, non-negotiable rules — budget, compliance, what's off-limits, approved tools only. Without Markers, AI will confidently break your business rules without even knowing it's doing it. Honestly the most important letter for keeping hallucinations from causing real damage.

questions.question: If you skip 'Role' in your P.R.O.M.P.T., what usually happens?
choices: AI gives a generic, non-expert response that needs heavy rework
AI asks you a clarifying question
AI defaults to the most recent role from your last session
questions.correct_answer: AI gives a generic, non-expert response that needs heavy rework
questions.explanation: Without Role, AI defaults to generic 'helpful assistant' mode — broad, surface-level, not specialized at all. Saying 'act as a senior payments architect with 10 years at FIS' completely changes the depth, vocabulary, everything. Same model, same prompt, just swap Role — night and day difference.

questions.question: Which two parts of P.R.O.M.P.T. control the actual shape AI hands back to you?
questions.explanation: Output sets the format — markdown table, JSON, React component, whatever. Pattern sets the internal structure — day-by-day, header-form-footer, etc. Together, they make the output ready to actually use, not ready to rewrite. Purpose and Role are the what and who. Marker and Tone are the rules and the vibe.

questions.question: In a typical OrchestrAI day, when does the business owner actually see a real working screen?
choices: End of the first sprint, around day 10
Same day as intent capture — around 11:30 AM
questions.correct_answer: Same day as intent capture — around 11:30 AM
questions.explanation: 9 AM intent capture, 10:30 first generation cycle, 11:30 you're showing a live screen to the business owner. That's the Mission Control rhythm — quick decision bursts, long stretches of supervising, real working software by mid-morning, day one. Not a mockup. The actual thing.
